repairs.why: EXTRACT_ANALYSIS routes its stimulus to `passage`, which every renderer places BEFORE the stem. The stems said 'the following passage' / 'the passage below'. Only the passage-facing direction was changed; 'the questions below' and 'the questions that follow' are correct and untouched.

items.before: Read the passage below and answer the questions that follow.
items.after: Read the passage above and answer the questions that follow.

periods.activity_title: Opening the Play: Pre-Reading and Act I Aloud

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reflect and Respond (p.169): paired identification of stringed instruments by first letter.
Reflect and Respond (p.169): class discussion on musical preferences across generations.

time_bands.activity: Distribute instruments-identification handout from Reflect and Respond. Students work in pairs naming stringed instruments by their first letter, then share briefly with the class to surface prior knowledge about classical and Western instruments.

Whole-class open discussion on whether children and elders differ in their music choices. Invite two or three contrasting views and note key words — tradition, fusion, preference — on the board to anchor the play's central tension.

Role-assigned reading of Act I aloud: assign Shruti, Iqbal, Avinash, Peter, and a Narrator. Students read observing stage directions and asides, with the teacher pausing briefly to clarify any unfamiliar stage terminology.

periods.teacher_notes: The play opens in Iqbal's room during a fusion rehearsal; Shruti's distress at the newspaper review sets the dramatic tension for all three acts. Watch for students who read asides in the same tone as dialogue — stress that asides are the character's private thought, spoken past the other characters to the audience.

periods.activity_title: Acts II and III Aloud: Conflict, Confrontation, Reconciliation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reading for Meaning (p.174): complete Act I setting-and-character table with teacher check.
Check Your Understanding (p.178): complete Act II summary cloze from the word box.

homework.task_brief: Reflect and Respond (p.170): complete the figurative-phrases paragraph using the box.

time_bands.activity: Brief recap: teacher asks two students to name the four musicians and Shruti's dilemma from Act I, grounding the class in the events already read before moving on.

Role-assigned reading of Act II aloud — Shruti, Nabin, Leela, and Narrator parts assigned. Pause after Nabin leaves the table so students complete the Act I setting-and-character table (Reading for Meaning) in pairs before continuing.

Role-assigned reading of Act III aloud, students observing Nabin's physical responses — foot-tapping, clapping, aside about his own history. After reading, pairs complete the Act II summary cloze (Check Your Understanding) using the word box.
Quick whole-class check of cloze answers. Set the Reflect and Respond figurative-phrases paragraph as an unhurried home task, asking students to note which phrases are literal and which figurative.

periods.teacher_notes: Act II hinges on Nabin's cold dismissal — 'drowning your individual style in the hubbub of an orchestra' — and Act III on Leela's quiet revelation that Nabin himself defied his traditional vocalist family to take up the violin. Students often miss this parallel; a brief directed question after the read helps surface it. The cloze task is verified against the drama summary: absent-minded (1), courage (2), disapproval (3), plea (4), firm (5), scolded (6), clash (7), setback (8).

periods.activity_title: Close Reading: Extract Analysis and True–False Scrutiny

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Check Your Understanding (p.181): identify true statements about Act III events.
Critical Reflection (p.182–183): extract-based close-reading questions on both extracts.

time_bands.activity: Students individually attempt the true–false task (Check Your Understanding) on Act III events — Shruti's resolve, Nabin's praise, Leela's revelation, Nabin's admission. Pairs compare and justify each verdict to a partner before whole-class discussion.

Teacher reads Extract 1 from Critical Reflection aloud; students work in pairs on the MCQ, the meaning of 'the right way', the generational-gap fill-in, and Iqbal's assurance. Class shares responses, with emphasis on how word choice signals Shruti's dilemma.

Teacher reads Extract 2 aloud; students individually address the MCQ on Nabin's breakthrough, the dual meaning of 'lost', the 'duty' exclusion MCQ, and the inference about Shruti's future. Brief whole-class synthesis of what both extracts reveal about the theme of tradition versus modernity.

periods.teacher_notes: The true–false task has a common pitfall: statement 4 is false because Nabin defied his vocal family to take up the violin — he did not follow the family tradition. In Extract 2 the word 'lost' carries both emotional loss of identity and the fear of physical separation; both senses must be named. Encourage students to quote the play when justifying their answers.

periods.activity_title: Critical Reflection: Character, Theme, and Title Justification

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Critical Reflection (p.184): six extended-answer questions on title, characters, theme, and conclusion.

time_bands.activity: Teacher frames the six analytical questions — title justification, peer characters' values, Nabin's arc, Shruti's internal conflict, effectiveness of the conclusion, and cultural diversity. Students read all six silently and note one key argument they want to make for any two questions of their choice.

Small groups of three discuss their chosen questions, each student defending a distinct claim. Teacher circulates, prompting with: 'Which moment in the play is your evidence?' and 'How does that connect to the tradition-versus-modernity theme?'

Whole-class sharing: one group presents on title justification, a second on Nabin's character arc, a third on the effectiveness of the conclusion. Teacher models a concise evaluative response for the conclusion question, connecting Nabin's own history as the reason the resolution feels earned.

periods.teacher_notes: The title 'Twin Melodies' refers both literally to the fusion of classical and Western strands and metaphorically to the parallel journeys of Nabin (who once defied tradition for the violin) and Shruti (who now defies him for fusion). Students who read the title only literally will miss the second melody. The phrase 'each bay, its own wind' is the play's key statement of individual artistic paths and anchors any discussion of cultural diversity.

periods.activity_title: Language in Focus: Drama Terms, Fillers, Music Vocabulary, and Reported Speech

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.184): MCQ on the function of the dramatic aside.
Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.185): non-lexical fillers — purpose MCQ and emoticon-matching task.
Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.186): match seven music-related words to meanings.
Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.187): identify exclamatory sentences and convert to declarative reported form.

homework.task_brief: Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.186): write meanings of three underlined music phrases in context.

time_bands.activity: Teacher displays the aside from the play and poses the MCQ on its function. After a brief show-of-hands vote, unpack each option — enabling talk about the story, revealing inner thought, creating audience connection — and confirm that all three apply. Then introduce non-lexical fillers: students match whew, err, arrgh, hmmm to four emoticons, noting the one extra filler.

Pairs work through the music-vocabulary matching task — rhythm, tempo, bass, baritone, cacophony, pitch, scale — with access to their copies of Act III. Teacher circulates and draws attention to how cacophony and harmony function as contrasting values in the play itself.

Whole-class work on exclamatory-to-declarative conversion: teacher models converting Shruti's 'Oh, how much I enjoy performing this piece!' using 'exclaimed with delight', showing removal of interjection, exclamation mark, and quotation marks. Students then attempt the second sentence independently and share. Meanings of the three underlined phrases are set as an unhurried home task.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently confuse the aside (option iv is correct — all three functions apply) with a soliloquy; clarify that an aside is short and directed past other characters, not a long reflection. In the reported-speech conversion the key changes are pronoun shift and removal of interjection — students often retain the exclamation mark and quotation marks in written form.

periods.activity_title: Yazh Description: Listening Notes and Stress-and-Intonation Performance

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Listen and Respond (p.189): complete notes on the yazh — type, design, and varieties — in three words or fewer.
Speaking Activity (p.189–190): perform four play lines with indicated stress and intonation; discuss emotional impact.

time_bands.activity: Teacher shows students three images of stringed instruments and asks them to predict which could be the yazh, the ancient Indian harp described in the transcript. Students note their choice before listening begins.

Teacher reads the transcript aloud (Listen and Respond, p.189) at a measured pace — or plays the audio where available — while students complete the notes skeleton: instrument type, usage, resonator shape and material, stem-tip design, and the four variety names. A second reading allows students to fill gaps, using no more than three words per blank.

Speaking Activity: teacher models the first line from the play — 'I don't want papa to feel that I don't care about his opinions, because I do' — with stressed syllables marked. Students practise all four lines in pairs, experimenting with different stress placements to test how meaning and emotion shift. Pairs then perform their preferred reading for the class and explain their stress choices.

periods.teacher_notes: The transcript describes the yazh as the ancestor of the veena, named for the Yali carved on its stem tip; its resonator is boat-shaped, skin-covered, and wooden. Students often struggle to hear the four variety names — peacock, crocodile, fish, and bow-string — so a second reading is built into the plan. For the speaking task, 'Each bay, its own wind' carries the play's whole thematic weight in four words; encourage students to explore the pause and falling intonation that makes it land.

periods.activity_title: Writing a Play Script: Drafting, Peer Response, and Revision

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Writing Task (p.190–191): groups draft, peer-respond to, and revise a play script based on the Anuradha story-seed.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly introduces the Anuradha story-seed: a talented teenage tabla player, a disapproving vocalist father, a supportive mother and brother, and an imminent prestigious performance. Groups of four are formed; each group assigns roles — director, scribe, character voices, stage-directions writer — and spends this opening band noting their setting, three characters, and the central conflict.

Groups draft their script: speaker names followed by colons, stage directions in brackets, at least one aside for Anuradha, non-lexical fillers where appropriate, and ellipsis to mark pauses. Teacher circulates, prompting groups who default to prose narrative instead of dialogue, and checking that stage directions carry physical cues rather than repeat what the dialogue already says.

Groups swap drafts with an adjacent group for a brief peer-response round. Peer readers check: Is the setting stated? Does each speaker have a colon after the name? Is there at least one aside? Is an ellipsis used correctly? Groups return drafts with one specific note for improvement.

Groups apply the single peer note to revise their draft. The teacher selects one group to read a short excerpt aloud, highlighting a strong aside or a well-used non-lexical filler as a model for the class.

periods.teacher_notes: The play script draws on conventions introduced in the drama just read — aside, stage directions in brackets, colon format — so groups who attended the earlier read-aloud will have concrete models to borrow from. A common weakness is writing stage directions that explain emotion already clear in the dialogue; prompt groups to use directions for physical action instead.
materials: Lined paper or notebooks for drafting

periods.activity_title: Script Conventions, Indigenous Instruments, and Found-Object Rhythm

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Learning Beyond the Text (p.192): four questions on play-script conventions — inverted commas, colons, brackets, and stage directions.
Learning Beyond the Text (p.192): brief research and sharing on indigenous instruments from students' own regions.
Learning Beyond the Text (p.192): groups create and present a rhythm using found objects in the classroom.

time_bands.activity: Students re-examine sample dialogue from the play-script conventions task (Learning Beyond the Text), answering the four questions in pairs: why no inverted commas, where colons appear, what bracket content conveys, and how stage directions help actors. Pairs share one answer each; the teacher consolidates the norms on the board.

Quick-share circle: each student names one indigenous instrument from their region — material it is made from (bamboo, gourd, hide, shell) and the cultural occasion it accompanies. Teacher adds brief context on how these connect to the play's theme of roots and identity.

Groups of five select classroom objects — rulers, desktops, water bottles, hands — and create a short repeating rhythm. Each group presents their pattern to the class and names the 'instrument'. The activity closes with a brief reflection: how does making music from everyday materials echo the Recycled Orchestra of Cateura's story and the play's message that music transcends boundaries.

periods.teacher_notes: The script-conventions task grounds the grammar of drama writing — no inverted commas because speaker attribution replaces them; colons after character names; brackets for stage directions that guide actor movement and delivery. Students may not know indigenous instruments outside their own region; accept any named instrument with a brief description of its material and use.
materials: Any available classroom objects for the rhythm activity

items.source_lo: Student analyses character motivation, dramatic conflict, and thematic resolution by close-reading a play.
items.source_context: Nabin's rigid opposition to fusion music and his eventual transformation through hearing Shruti perform.
items.item_stem: In Act II, Nabin tells Shruti that performing fusion music means drowning her individual style in the hubbub of an orchestra. Which of the following best explains why Nabin holds this view at this point in the play?

options.label: A
options.text: He believes Shruti lacks the technical ability to play in an ensemble.

options.label: B
options.text: He has already attended a fusion concert and disliked the sound.

options.label: C
options.text: He is angry that Shruti spent his money on rehearsal sessions without telling him.

options.label: D
options.text: He values the distinctiveness of classical Hindustani music and fears fusion will dilute Shruti's artistic identity.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Suggests the student has confused Nabin's ideological objection with a skills assessment he never makes.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Suggests the student has invented a scene — Nabin explicitly refuses to attend even a rehearsal before deciding.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Suggests the student has focused on Leela's scolding about hidden sessions rather than Nabin's stated musical objection.

items.source_lo: Student analyses character motivation, dramatic conflict, and thematic resolution by close-reading a play.
items.source_context: Nabin's rigid opposition to fusion music and his eventual transformation through hearing Shruti perform.
items.item_stem:
Read the passage above and answer the questions that follow.

1. How does Leela's quiet revelation — that Nabin himself once defied his traditional vocalist family to take up the violin — change the audience's understanding of Nabin's earlier harshness? What irony does this create?
2. By the end of Act III, Nabin admits, 'I underestimated the power of our own music. I was afraid you would be lost to us.' Analyse what this admission reveals about the true source of his fear throughout the play.
3. The play ends with Nabin declaring, 'Each bay, its own wind.' Evaluate how effectively this single phrase resolves the play's central conflict between tradition and modernity.
items.visual_stimulus: Act III — Iqbal's house. Mid-rehearsal, Nabin and Leela arrive unannounced. The music draws Nabin in; he is seen tapping his feet, then clapping furiously, his face alight with pride. He praises Shruti for never losing sight of the raga notes, then offers the children his music room for regular practice. In a quiet aside, Leela reveals to Shruti that Nabin had once defied his own family — a traditional vocalist household — to take up the violin, and had worked his fingers to the bone to succeed.

expected_elements: Leela's revelation creates dramatic irony: Nabin repeated the very defiance he punished.
His fear was loss of Shruti's identity to fusion, not mere conservatism.
Admission shows pride in classical music driving the fear, not hostility to Shruti.
'Each bay, its own wind' honours individual artistic paths within a shared tradition.
Student should evaluate whether the phrase is a sufficient or too-neat resolution.

items.source_lo: Student demonstrates focused listening by taking structured notes from an oral description of a musical instrument.
items.source_context: A musician's spoken description of the yazh — its design, resonator, tuning, and named varieties.
items.item_stem:
Listen to the description of the yazh and decide whether each statement is true or false. Write T or F beside each statement and give a one-sentence reason from the description.
(1) The yazh is named after the Yali because its resonator is carved into the shape of that mythological animal.
(2) The yazh is considered an ancestor of the modern-day veena.
(3) The instrument was tuned using either pegs or movable rings of gut on the strings.
(4) All varieties of the yazh share the same resonator shape.

options.text: All varieties of the yazh share the same resonator shape.
The instrument was tuned using either pegs or movable rings of gut on the strings.
The yazh is considered an ancestor of the modern-day veena.
The yazh is named after the Yali because its resonator is carved into the shape of that mythological animal.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: (1) F — the Yali is carved on the tip of the stem, not the resonator. (2) T — the transcript states the yazh is the ancestor of the modern-day veena. (3) T — the transcript says it was tuned by either pegs or rings of gut moved up and down the strings. (4) F — design variations gave the instrument different names (peacock, crocodile, fish, bow-string), indicating differing forms.

items.source_lo: Student demonstrates focused listening by taking structured notes from an oral description of a musical instrument.
items.source_context: A musician's spoken description of the yazh — its design, resonator, tuning, and named varieties.
items.item_stem: After listening to the description of the yazh, a student writes in her notes: 'The yazh had four named varieties, each based on a different animal or object — this shows the instrument evolved differently across regions or makers.' Using evidence from the description, explain whether this inference is well supported. What does the existence of four named varieties suggest about the yazh's history or cultural spread?

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The inference is well supported: the four variety names — peacock, crocodile, fish, and bow-string yazh — reflect design differences rather than a single fixed form, suggesting the instrument adapted across different makers or regional contexts.

items.source_lo: Student uses stress and intonation to convey character emotion and dramatic meaning in spoken performance.
items.source_context: Performing selected lines from the play with discussed stress and intonation to explore their emotional impact.
items.item_stem: Read aloud Shruti's line: 'I don't want papa to feel that I don't care about his opinions, because I do.' Perform it twice — first stressing the word 'don't' in the first clause, then stressing the word 'do' at the end. Describe how the emotional meaning shifts between the two readings.

expected_elements: Student performs both readings with clearly audible stress difference.
First reading emphasises Shruti's anxiety about appearing disrespectful.
Second reading emphasises her genuine love and respect for her father.
Student articulates how the same words convey different emotional priorities.
Delivery shows awareness of pause or pace change alongside stress shift.

items.source_lo: Student uses stress and intonation to convey character emotion and dramatic meaning in spoken performance.
items.source_context: Performing selected lines from the play with discussed stress and intonation to explore their emotional impact.
items.item_stem: In the play, Nabin tells Shruti that playing fusion music means drowning her individual style in an orchestra, while by the end he declares, 'Each bay, its own wind.' Argue, with reasons drawn from the play, whether Nabin's change of heart is believable or whether it happens too quickly to be convincing. Be prepared to respond to a counter-argument from a classmate.

expected_elements: Student takes a clear position — believable or too sudden — and states it.
Argument cites at least one specific moment: foot-tapping, Leela's revelation, or Nabin's own history with the violin.
Student acknowledges the counter-argument and responds to it with a reason.
Delivery is audible, measured, and uses appropriate formal register.
Conclusion links back to the tradition-versus-modernity theme of the play.

items.source_lo: Student writes an original play script using dramatic conventions — asides, stage directions, and non-lexical fillers — as the vehicle.
items.source_context: A young musician's conflict with a disapproving parent over performing at a civic youth music festival.
items.item_stem: Write an invitation to the parents of participating students for a youth music festival at your school. Include: the name and date of the event, the programme (two classical and one fusion item), a note explaining that students have rehearsed under a music teacher's guidance, and a request for the parents to attend and show their support. Use formal invitation format.

expected_elements: Formal invitation format: heading, date, venue, and polite salutation.
Programme details name at least two items, mixing classical and fusion genres.
Mention of teacher-supervised rehearsal adds credibility and reassures parents.
Request for parental presence is expressed politely and with a stated reason.
Language is consistently formal; spelling and punctuation are accurate.

items.source_lo: Student writes an original play script using dramatic conventions — asides, stage directions, and non-lexical fillers — as the vehicle.
items.source_context: A young musician's conflict with a disapproving parent over performing at a civic youth music festival.
items.item_stem: Write a short play script (one scene, approximately one page) in which a student tries to convince a sceptical school principal to allow a fusion music performance at the annual day. Your script must include: a setting described in a stage direction, at least one aside for the student character, a non-lexical filler to show nervousness, and a moment where the principal's position begins to soften. Follow play-script formatting conventions throughout.

expected_elements: Play-script format: character name followed by colon, no inverted commas for dialogue.
Opening stage direction establishes the setting clearly in square brackets.
At least one aside marked in brackets shows the student's inner thought.
A non-lexical filler (err, hmm, or similar) signals the character's nervousness.
Principal's softening is shown through a line of dialogue or a stage direction, not just stated.

items.source_context: Music-register vocabulary and reported-speech conversion drawn from dialogues in the play.
items.item_stem: Match each music-related word from Column A with its correct meaning in Column B.
items.visual_stimulus:
Column A | Column B
tempo | (i) the perceived frequency of a sound — how high or low it is
cacophony | (ii) the speed or pace at which a piece of music is played
baritone | (iii) a mixture of loud, unpleasant sounds
scale | (iv) a male voice range between the higher and lower registers
pitch | (v) a series of musical notes moving upwards or downwards

answer_key.right: (ii) the speed or pace at which a piece of music is played
(iii) a mixture of loud, unpleasant sounds
(iv) a male voice range between the higher and lower registers
(v) a series of musical notes moving upwards or downwards
(i) the perceived frequency of a sound — how high or low it is

items.source_lo: Student applies domain vocabulary and exclamatory-to-reported-speech transformation using drama as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Music-register vocabulary and reported-speech conversion drawn from dialogues in the play.
items.item_stem:
The sentences below are taken from the world of the play. Convert each exclamatory sentence into reported (indirect) speech, using the reporting verb and the subject given in brackets. Remove the interjection, exclamation mark, and quotation marks, and make all necessary grammatical changes.

1. 'Wah, how soulful! You all have done a wonderful job!' (Leela / exclaimed with delight that)
2. 'Incredible — each note was exactly where it belonged!' (Nabin / exclaimed admiringly that)
3. 'Oh no, my raga will go down the drain if I miss this rehearsal!' (Shruti / exclaimed anxiously that)

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. Leela exclaimed with delight that they had all done a wonderful job. 2. Nabin exclaimed admiringly that each note had been exactly where it belonged. 3. Shruti exclaimed anxiously that her raga would go down the drain if she missed that rehearsal.

items.source_lo: Student explores cultural heritage through play-script conventions and indigenous musical traditions as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Script formatting conventions and indigenous instruments crafted from natural materials in students' own regions.
items.item_stem: A student reads a play for the first time and is puzzled: 'Why doesn't the playwright use inverted commas for dialogue the way a story writer does?' Write two to three sentences explaining the formatting conventions of a play script — why inverted commas are absent, what the colon after a character's name does, and what stage directions in brackets tell us.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: In a play script, the character's name before a colon already identifies the speaker, so inverted commas are unnecessary. The colon signals that what follows is spoken aloud by that character. Stage directions in brackets describe physical action, movement, or tone — information the actor and director need that is not part of the spoken dialogue.

items.source_lo: Student explores cultural heritage through play-script conventions and indigenous musical traditions as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Script formatting conventions and indigenous instruments crafted from natural materials in students' own regions.
items.item_stem: Choose one indigenous musical instrument from your region that is made from a natural material — bamboo, gourd, animal hide, shell, or any other. Write a short project plan (one paragraph) that outlines: (a) the name of the instrument and the material it is made from, (b) the cultural occasion or community where it is traditionally played, (c) how you would find out more about it — one person you could speak to or one source you could consult — and (d) one way the instrument connects to the theme of roots and identity explored in Twin Melodies.

expected_elements: Instrument named with its natural material clearly identified.
Cultural occasion or community context described in specific terms.
A plausible research step named — a person, a library source, or a community event.
Connection to roots and identity draws a genuine parallel with the play's themes.
Writing is organised as a paragraph with clear, logical sequencing of the four points.
